card_quote: I pick things that will make the recipient laugh on the day, and I buy several small gifts at once, so each one has a low budget.
how_read: Dipped in. Read the How to play page, did Round 1 on the sofa after the kids were in bed, then Round 2 mostly flicking for something funny to read out to my other half. Had a look at the game-night page at the back to see if it would work on Boxing Day. I would not read it cover to cover, it's for my brother, not me.

w1_friction.note: AI wrote it. Fine, but I would not put that on a gift tag.
w1_friction.quote: the entries were drafted with AI tools

w1_friction.note: Three verdicts, sure or guessing, stars, a score table. That's a lot of rules for a stocking filler.
w1_friction.quote: tick whether you are sure or guessing

w1_friction.note: A whole page of small print for one bath. He'll read the top line and the Tell someone bit and that's it.
I said folklore on the apple and now it's TRUE. Feels like a trick question, which is annoying.
w1_friction.quote: Only the apple hitting his head was added afterward.

w1_friction.note: Disputed on Murphy's law? That's a cop-out. I want an answer to shout at the table.
w1_friction.quote: Who first said it, and in what words, is not settled.

w1_friction.note: Goodhart and a monetary-policy paper. My brother would be asleep by line three.
w1_friction.quote: a monetary cousin of the Lucas critique

w1_friction.note: Pedantic. Everyone says impostor syndrome, my sister's a nurse, nobody cares which word.
w1_friction.quote: “Syndrome” is popular usage, not their term

w1_best.why: Blood, toil, tears and sweat. Four things, not three. I can say that over the turkey.
Everyone knows Eureka in the bath and it's not true. Easy one to start with.
The apple on the head one, I've heard it debunked on QI and it still made me smile.
Crud, not crap. Funny that the swearword got sharper in the retelling.
Babylonians had it a thousand years before Pythagoras. Good dinner fact.

w1_flat.why: Latin sentences and a friar. No laugh anywhere.
Neurons and a rhyme, I lost it halfway down.
Monetary policy. For a stocking? No.
Hanlon, Heinlein, Bloch. Too many names for something so short-lived.
A word fight, phenomenon versus syndrome. Nobody at my table would care.

w1_review.headline: Clever, but it's homework not a laugh
w1_review.body: Nice idea and the dedication page made me smile, but every answer is a full page of small print and there are hardly any jokes. Good for the sort of person who watches QI and likes being right, less good for someone who just wants to open it on Christmas morning. I'd pick it for one particular brother, not for everyone on my list. Bottom line: a decent stocking filler for a know-it-all, if the price is right.

w2_review_first: It's a clever book for a clever person who likes being the one who knows. I'd say it's more homework than laugh, so only get it for someone who already enjoys that sort of thing, like my brother who watches QI.

w2_lost.why: Ockham and a Latin sentence. That's where I started flicking.
Hanlon's razor, three names and a 1980 book. Page after page of the same shape.
Godwin and Usenet, I had no idea what Usenet was and the page didn't help.

w2_read_aloud.why: Short, surprising and everybody has said it wrong at some point.
Crud versus crap gets a laugh. People love a swearword.
The bath one is the one everyone thinks they know, so there's a groan when it's wrong.
Twain or Einstein, and it was neither. People guess the famous names at me.
A bump on the head is slapstick, the kids would even follow that one.

w2_cut.why: Latin and a friar, no one reads that out.
It's the same answer as the one before. Padding.
Another quote that wasn't Twain. By then I had the trick.

w2_book2: If the next one is the same wall of small print with no jokes, or costs more than a normal stocking filler.
